Assume the RD identification assumptions from the section hold, except where a question asks you to assess them.

### 5. Read the effect from a graph

In Panel A, patients arriving before time zero receive traditional flow; patients arriving at or after zero receive split flow. In Panel B, patients receive treatment when their risk score is at least 20. The curves show mean observed outcomes.

![](images/04c-rd-exercise-curves.svg){width=850 fig-align="center" fig-alt="Two gridded RD plots. Panel A shows mean time to disposition with a treatment cutoff at zero. Panel B shows mean symptom score with a treatment cutoff at 20."}

a. In Panel A, estimate the local average treatment effect of split flow on time to disposition at time zero.

b. In Panel B, estimate the local average treatment effect on symptom score at risk score 20.

c. Do these comparisons also identify the average treatment effect for all patients?

<div class="response-space"></div>

::: {.answer-block}
**Solution**

a. The mean falls from 100 to 90 minutes at the cutoff. The local average treatment effect of split flow is $90-100=-10$ minutes at time zero.

b. The mean rises from 6 to 10 at the cutoff. The local average treatment effect is $10-6=4$ symptom-score units at risk score 20.

c. No. They identify average effects at the cutoffs. Extending them to all patients requires additional assumptions.
:::

### 6. Estimate the jump from a table

In a fictional oncology clinic, patients with a cancer risk score of at least 20 receive an additional therapy. Patients below 20 receive usual care alone. The outcome is tumor diameter eight weeks later; smaller is better. Each row is one patient, and the scores and data are made up.

| Risk score | Tumor diameter (mm) |
|---:|---:|
| 16 | 12 |
| 17 | 12 |
| 18 | 8 |
| 19 | 8 |
| 21 | 4 |
| 22 | 4 |
| 23 | 6 |
| 24 | 6 |

A bandwidth $h$ includes scores from $20-h$ to $20+h$, including the endpoints. Estimate the local average treatment effect of adding the therapy at score 20 by subtracting the untreated sample mean from the treated sample mean.

a. Estimate the effect using $h=4$.

b. Estimate the effect using $h=2$.

c. How many observations does each bandwidth include?

<div class="response-space"></div>

::: {.answer-block}
**Solution**

a. The untreated mean is $(12+12+8+8)/4=10$ mm. The treated mean is $(4+4+6+6)/4=5$ mm. The estimated local average treatment effect at score 20 is $5-10=-5$ mm.

b. The untreated mean is 8 mm and the treated mean is 4 mm. The estimated local average treatment effect at score 20 is $4-8=-4$ mm.

c. The wider bandwidth includes eight patients; the narrower one includes four.
:::

### 7. Use fitted regression lines

Split flow begins at noon. Let $r$ be arrival time in hours, so noon is $r=12$. Using arrivals within one hour of noon, researchers fit:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Before noon:}\quad \hat m_0(r)&=100+6(r-12),\\[0.5em]
\text{After noon:}\quad \hat m_1(r)&=90+2(r-12).
\end{aligned}
$$

The outcome is time to disposition in minutes.

a. What does each line predict at noon?

b. Estimate the local average treatment effect of split flow at noon.

c. What is one benefit and one risk of using a wider bandwidth?

d. Researchers add a quadratic term in $R$ to each model and obtain a larger $R^2$ and a smaller AIC. Does this establish that their estimate of the local average treatment effect is more accurate? Explain.

<div class="response-space"></div>

::: {.answer-block}
**Solution**

a. At $r=12$, the predictions are 100 minutes under traditional flow and 90 under split flow.

b. The estimated local average treatment effect at noon is $90-100=-10$ minutes.

c. A wider bandwidth includes more observations, which can improve precision. The fitted line may approximate the mean curve poorly over the wider range, introducing bias.

d. No. A larger $R^2$ or smaller AIC does not establish that the fitted curves predict more accurately at the cutoff. Use boundary-oriented cross-validation to assess predictions on observations left out of fitting.
:::

### 8. Check a placement-test design

Students scoring below 80 must take developmental mathematics. Students scoring at least 80 skip it. The outcome is credits completed in the following year.

a. Mean credits are 18 just below 80 and 22 just above. Estimate the local average treatment effect of developmental mathematics at score 80.

b. Scores pile up at exactly 80. Why would this concern you?

c. Women make up 50% of students just below 80 and 70% just above. Why does this raise doubts about the comparison?

d. Only second-attempt scores were recorded. How could different retake rates by gender produce the difference in part c?

<div class="response-space"></div>

::: {.answer-block}
**Solution**

a. Treated students are below the cutoff. The estimated local average treatment effect at score 80 is $18-22=-4$ credits.

b. Students may be getting scores changed to avoid the course. Those who obtain changes may differ from those who remain below 80. Scoring, appeals, and retake rules need investigation.

c. The groups differ in a pretreatment characteristic at the cutoff. This suggests sorting or sample selection, although sampling noise could also produce a difference.

d. If retaking depends on gender and the first score, the students with recorded second scores may have different gender compositions on the two sides.
:::

### 9. A fuzzy treatment rule

A clinic recommends treatment at a risk score of 20. Patients can decline. Larger symptom scores mean worse symptoms.

| Just below or above 20 | Treatment uptake | Mean symptom score |
|---|---:|---:|
| Below | 0.2 | 15 |
| Above | 0.6 | 13 |

Assume the fuzzy RD assumptions from the section hold.

a. Calculate the jump in mean symptoms and the jump in treatment uptake.

b. Estimate the local average treatment effect by dividing the outcome jump by the treatment jump.

c. Which patients does this effect describe?

<div class="response-space"></div>

::: {.answer-block}
**Solution**

a. The outcome jump is $13-15=-2$ symptom-score units. The treatment jump is $0.6-0.2=0.4$.

b. The estimated local average treatment effect is $-2/0.4=-5$ symptom-score units among compliers at risk score 20.

c. Compliers at risk score 20: patients who would take treatment when eligible for the recommendation and would not take it without eligibility. Treatment reduces their mean symptom score by 5 units.
:::
